scenes.title: CROSS JOIN
scenes.narration: A CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product, pairing every row of the left table with every row of the right table.

scenes.title: What CROSS JOIN does
bullets: Pairs every left row with every right row.
Has no ON clause and no match condition.
Result size equals rows_left times rows_right.
scenes.narration: A cross join combines each row of one table with each row of the other. It has no ON clause because there is no matching condition to satisfy. The output size is simply the number of left rows multiplied by the number of right rows.

scenes.title: Every size and color combination
scenes.narration: This pairs every size with every color to enumerate all product variants. If there are three sizes and four colors, the result contains twelve rows, one for each combination. Cross joins are the clean way to generate all possible pairings when you deliberately want them.

scenes.title: Building a date spine
steps: LEFT JOIN sales onto that grid.
scenes.narration: A common data-engineering use is building a complete date spine so every store has a row for every day. You cross join a list of dates with the list of stores to form the full grid, then left join the actual sales onto it. Days with no sales then show up explicitly as zero rather than being missing.

scenes.title: Intentional vs accidental

left.title: Intentional CROSS JOIN
points: Row count is expected and controlled.

right.title: Accidental Cartesian
points: Comma join with a missing condition.
A common source of slow, wrong queries.

scenes.narration: An intentional cross join is written explicitly because you truly want every combination and the row count is expected. An accidental Cartesian product usually comes from listing tables with a comma but forgetting the join condition, causing counts to explode. That mistake is a frequent cause of slow queries and inflated results.

scenes.title: Spotting a missing join condition
scenes.code:
-- Accidental Cartesian: no join condition
SELECT *
FROM customers, orders;

-- Correct: join on the key
SELECT *
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
scenes.narration: The first query lists two tables with a comma and no condition, so it silently returns every customer paired with every order. The second query adds an explicit ON clause so each customer is matched only to their own orders. Always supply a join condition unless you genuinely intend a Cartesian product.

scenes.text: If a result set is far larger than expected, suspect a missing join condition producing an accidental Cartesian product.
scenes.narration: When results balloon far beyond what you expected, suspect a missing join condition creating an accidental Cartesian product.
